o: We must split `n` into the fewest pieces, each being `digit × 10^p`. Each decimal digit of `n` produces exactly one nonzero component, and you can never merge two digits into one component, so the minimum count equals the number of nonzero digits. For `n = 537` the digits 5, 3, 7 give `[500, 30, 7]`; for `102` the zero digit is skipped giving `[100, 2]`. With `n ≤ 10^9` there are at most 10 digits, so any linear scan works.
k: The optimal decomposition is forced: every nonzero decimal digit becomes its own component.

a.i: Peel digits off `n` from the least significant side, multiplying a power-of-ten tracker. Collect nonzero contributions and reverse at the end to get descending order.
s: Initialize power p = 1 and an empty list.
While n > 0, take d = n % 10; if d != 0 push d * p.
Divide n by 10 and multiply p by 10.
Reverse the list and return it.
a.t: O(log₁₀ n) — one pass over the digits
a.sp: O(log₁₀ n) — output holds at most 10 numbers

a.i: Convert `n` to a string; each nonzero character at position i contributes `int(ch) * 10^(len-1-i)`. Reading left to right naturally yields descending order.
s: For each character, if nonzero append digit times the matching power of ten.

w: Either approach is fine in an interview; the math version avoids string/pow overhead. Pitfall: forgetting to skip zero digits or forgetting to reverse in Approach 1. Follow-up: what if components had to be returned in ascending order?
